en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 126, the Bhūmija Sutta.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Bhūmija dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Prince Jayasena. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Prince Jayasena approached the Venerable Bhūmija and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Prince Jayasena said to the Venerable Bhūmija:
"Master Bhūmija, there are certain recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
'Even if they lead the holy life with the expectation of a result, they are incapable of attaining any fruit.'"
‘If they lead the holy life having formed expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
if they lead the holy life having formed neither expectations nor non-expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
and if they lead the holy life having formed neither expectation nor non-expectation, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.’”
“In this case, Master Bhūmija, what does the Teacher say, and what does he proclaim?
“Prince, I have not heard this directly from the Blessed One, nor have I received it directly from him.
However, it is possible that the Blessed One would answer thus:”
‘If they practice the holy life without proper method while harboring expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
if they practice the holy life without proper method while harboring no expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
and if they practice the holy life without proper method while harboring both expectations and no expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.’
Whether they practice the holy life with improper attention, having formed either a hope or no hope for the result, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
But if they practice the holy life with proper attention, whether they have formed a hope or have no hope for the result, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
‘Whether one forms the aspiration or does not form the aspiration, if one leads the holy life with wise reflection, one is capable of attaining the fruit;
whether one forms neither the aspiration nor the non-aspiration, if one leads the holy life with wise reflection, one is capable of attaining the fruit.
Prince, I did not hear this directly from the Blessed One, nor was it received directly from him.
"But it is indeed possible that the Blessed One would answer in such a way.
"If Master Bhūmija’s teacher speaks thus and declares thus, then surely Master Bhūmija’s teacher stands as if striking the very crowns of the heads of all those common recluses and brahmins.
Then Prince Jayasena served the Venerable Bhūmija with his own dish of rice.
Then, after his meal, having returned from his alms round, the Venerable Bhūmija approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Bhūmija said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I went to the residence of Prince Jayasena. Having arrived, I sat down on the prepared seat.
Then, Bhante, Prince Jayasena approached me; having approached, he exchanged greetings with me.
When we had concluded our polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Bhante, Prince Jayasena said this to me:”
“Master Bhūmija, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘Even if they lead the holy life with aspiration, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
even if they lead the holy life without aspiration...’”
‘Whether they practice the holy life by forming the aspiration “I shall be” or “I shall not be,” they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
or whether they practice the holy life by neither forming the aspiration “I shall be” nor “I shall not be,” they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
‘In this regard, Master Bhūmija, what does your teacher say, what does he proclaim?’”
When this was said, venerable sir, I said this to Prince Jayasena:
“I have not heard this from the Blessed One’s own presence, nor have I received it directly from him.
However, it is possible that the Blessed One would explain it in this way:”
If they practice the holy life unreasonably while forming expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
if they practice the holy life unreasonably while forming no expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
and if they practice the holy life unreasonably while both forming and not forming expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
Whether they practice the holy life with improper attention, having formed either a hope or a lack of hope, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
But if they practice the holy life with proper attention, whether they have formed a hope or a lack of hope, they are capable of attaining the fruit. ... [and so on] ...
even if they have formed no hope at all.
"Whether they form the perception of existence, or the perception of non-existence...
or even whether they form neither the perception of existence nor the perception of non-existence, if they lead the holy life with wise reflection, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
"Prince, I have not heard this directly from the Blessed One, nor have I received it directly from him."
"But it is indeed possible that the Blessed One would answer in this way.
"If Master Bhūmija’s teacher speaks thus and declares thus, then surely Master Bhūmija’s teacher stands as if striking the very crowns of the heads of all those ordinary recluses and brahmins.
"Venerable sir, if I were asked thus and answered thus, would I be speaking in accordance with what the Blessed One has said, and not misrepresenting him?"
“...and do I misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, do I explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma,
and does no legitimate criticism or counter-argument find ground for reproach?
“Certainly, Bhūmija, when questioned thus and answering in this way, you have spoken as I would say, and you have not misrepresented me.”
"You misrepresent me with what is untrue, you explain in a way that is contrary to the Dhamma,
and no legitimate point of criticism can be found for reproach.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, Bhūmija, hold wrong view, wrong intention, and wrong speech..."
Those who have wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—
if they practice the holy life while forming a wish for results, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
if they practice the holy life without forming a wish for results, they are still incapable of attaining the fruit.
Whether they practice the holy life with expectations or without expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
whether they practice the holy life neither with expectations nor without expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
For what reason?
This, Bhūmija, is not the way for the attainment of fruit.
Just as if, Bhūmija, a man needing oil, seeking oil, wandering in search of oil, were to fill a bowl with sand and press it repeatedly while sprinkling it with water—
even if he were to do so with hope— having filled a bowl with sand and pressed it repeatedly while sprinkling it with water, he would be incapable of attaining oil.
If one were to form no expectation at all, pour sand into a bowl, and press it down repeatedly while sprinkling it with water, one would be incapable of obtaining oil.
If one were to both form an expectation and form no expectation, pour sand into a bowl, and press it down repeatedly while sprinkling it with water, one would be incapable of obtaining oil.
If one were to neither form an expectation nor form no expectation, pour sand into a bowl, and press it down repeatedly while sprinkling it with water, one would be incapable of obtaining oil.
And why is that? Because, Bhūmija, this is not the proper method for obtaining oil.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever ascetics or brahmins hold wrong views and have wrong intentions...
Those who possess wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—
if they practice the holy life while forming aspirations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit;
if they practice the holy life without forming aspirations, they are still incapable of attaining the fruit.
Whether they practice the holy life with expectations or without expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
Whether they practice the holy life neither with expectations nor without expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit. Why is that?
This, Bhūmija, is not the way to attain the fruit.
Just as if, Bhūmija, a man seeking milk, looking for milk, wandering in search of milk, were to pull at the horns of a cow with a young calf from behind;
even if he did so with hope, by pulling at the horns of a cow with a young calf, he would be incapable of attaining milk.
If, having formed no expectation,
or having formed both expectation and non-expectation,
or even having formed neither expectation nor non-expectation, one were to pull at a young calf by its horns, it would be impossible to obtain milk.
And why is that? Because, Bhūmija, this is not the proper method for obtaining milk.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever ascetics or brahmins hold wrong views... [and so on].

If they practice the holy life with wrong concentration, whether they do so with expectation or without expectation— or both with expectation and without expectation— they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
Even if they practice the holy life by making a distinction between dwelling together and dwelling apart, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
Why is that? Because this, Bhūmija, is not the proper method for attaining the fruit.

"Just as, Bhūmija, a man needing butter, seeking butter, wandering in search of butter, might pour water into a bowl and churn it with a churning-stick—even if he were to do so with hope, pouring water into a bowl and churning it with a churning-stick, he would be incapable of obtaining butter;
and even if he were to do so without hope... [and so on]."
Whether one forms the perception of existence or non-existence...

or even whether one forms the perception of neither existence nor non-existence, if one were to pour water into a jar and churn it with a churning-stick, one would be incapable of obtaining butter. Why is that?
This, Bhūmija, is not the proper way to obtain butter.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever ascetics or brahmins hold wrong views...
[and so on] ...up to those with wrong concentration, even if they lead the holy life with such aspirations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
If they lead the holy life having formed no expectations, or having formed both expectations and no expectations,
or having formed neither expectations nor no expectations, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
And why is that? Because, Bhūmija, this is not the proper method for attaining the fruit.
It is just as if, Bhūmija, a man needing fire, seeking fire, wandering in search of fire, were to take a wet, sap-filled piece of wood as an upper drill-stick and churn it.

Even if one were to form the aspiration and, taking a moist, sapwood fire-drill, were to churn it, one would be incapable of obtaining fire; even if one were not to form the aspiration … [and so on] … even if one were to both form the aspiration and not form the aspiration … [and so on] …
Even if one were to make an effort both here and there, and taking a wet, sap-filled piece of wood as the upper fire-drill, were to churn it, one would be incapable of obtaining fire.
Why is that? Because, Bhūmija, this is not the proper method for obtaining fire.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever recluses or brahmins hold wrong view ... [and so on] ...
up to those who possess wrong concentration, even if they lead the holy life with a longing for the goal, they are incapable of attaining its fruit;
even if they lead the holy life without a longing for the goal ... [and so on].

Whether they practice the holy life having formed the perception of existence, or the perception of non-existence, or even the perception of neither existence nor non-existence, they are incapable of attaining the fruit.
For what reason?
This, Bhūmija, is not the way for the attainment of the fruit.
For whatever recluses or brahmins, Bhūmija, possess right view, right intention, right speech, right action,
right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— even if they were to form a mere wish— [they would attain it].
If they lead the holy life with expectation, they are capable of attaining the fruit;
if they lead the holy life even without expectation, they are capable of attaining the fruit;
if they lead the holy life both with and without expectation, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
Whether they live together or separately, if they lead the holy life, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
Why is that? Because this, Bhūmija, is the source for the attainment of the fruit.
"Just as if, Bhūmija, a man needing oil, seeking oil, wandering in search of oil, were to pour sesame paste into a trough and press it repeatedly while sprinkling it with water.
If he were to do so with expectation, pouring sesame paste into a trough and pressing it repeatedly while sprinkling it with water, he would be capable of obtaining oil;
and even if he were to do so without expectation... [and so on].
Whether one forms the perception of existence or non-existence...

or even whether one forms the perception of neither-existence-nor-non-existence, if one were to pour sesame meal into a vat and press it down, sprinkling it repeatedly with water, one would be capable of obtaining oil. Why is that?
"This, Bhūmija, is the source for the attainment of oil.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever ascetics or brahmins have right view... [and so on] ...up to...
right concentration, if they lead the holy life even while forming an aspiration, they are capable of attaining the fruit."
If they practice the holy life having formed no expectation, or having formed both expectation and no expectation,
or having formed neither expectation nor no expectation, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
For what reason?
Because this, Bhūmija, is the means for the attainment of the fruit.
Just as if, Bhūmija, a man seeking milk, searching for milk, wandering in quest of milk, were to pull at the udder of a cow that has a young calf.
If one were to form an expectation and pull a cow with a young calf from her udder, one would be capable of obtaining milk;
if one were to form no expectation … [and so on] … if one were to form both an expectation and no expectation … [and so on].
Even if one were to make it neither stay nor go away, and were to pull a cow with a young calf by the udder, she would be capable of yielding milk.
Why is that? Because, Bhūmija, this is the source from which milk comes.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever recluses or brahmins have right view … [and so on] … up to … right concentration,
whether they form an aspiration or do not form an aspiration … [and so on] … [they all attain final knowledge].

Whether they practice the holy life having formed the perception of existence, or the perception of non-existence, or even the perception of neither existence nor non-existence, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
For what reason?
This is the source, Bhūmija, for the attainment of the fruit. Just as if, Bhūmija,
a man needing butter, seeking butter, wandering in search of butter, were to pour curd into a jar and churn it with a churning-stick—
even if he were to do so with hope, pouring curd into a jar and churning it with a churning-stick, he would be capable of attaining butter.
If one were to pour curd into a jar and stir it with a ladle, even without forming the expectation,
or even while forming both the expectation and the non-expectation, or even without forming either the expectation or the non-expectation, one would be capable of obtaining butter.
For what reason?
Because this, Bhūmija, is the source for obtaining butter.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever ascetics or brahmins possess right view... [and so forth].
If they lead the holy life with right concentration while forming an aspiration, they are capable of attaining the fruit;
if they do so without forming an aspiration…; if they do so both forming and not forming an aspiration…; [in all cases,] they are capable of attaining the fruit.
Whether they lead the holy life together or separately, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
Why is that? Because this, Bhūmija, is the source for the attainment of the fruit.
"Just as, Bhūmija, a man seeking fire, searching for fire, wandering in quest of fire, might take a dry stick and an upper fire-stick and rub them together—
whether he does so with expectation or without expectation."
Whether one forms the perception of existence or non-existence,

or even the perception of neither existence nor non-existence, if one were to take dry wood from a brush-heap and, using it as the upper fire-drill, twirl it, it would be possible for a fire to be produced. Why is that?
This, Bhūmija, is the source for the attainment of fire.
In the same way, Bhūmija, whatever ascetics or brahmins possess right view...
[and so on] ...right concentration, if they lead the holy life even while forming a wish, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
If they lead the holy life without forming expectations, they are capable of attaining the fruit;
if they lead the holy life both forming and not forming expectations, they are capable of attaining the fruit;
and if they lead the holy life neither forming nor not forming expectations, they are capable of attaining the fruit.
"And why is that? Because this, Bhūmija, is the means for attaining the fruit.

If these four similes had occurred to you, Bhūmija, regarding Prince Jayasena, it would not be surprising if Prince Jayasena were to place his confidence in you, and being confident, he would show his confidence to you."
“But from where, Bhante, would these four similes occur to me—unprecedented, never heard before, just as they have occurred to the Blessed One?
This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Bhūmija, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Bhūmijasutta, the sixth, is finished.
